newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan exiles in U.S. face mass deportation.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan exiles in U.S. face mass deportation.

text.p: Thousands of Nicaraguans living in the United States face deportation as new U.S. immigration laws are put into effect, despite official assurances to the contrary, a top Nicaraguan exile said on Sunday.

More than 20,000 Nicaraguans in the Miami region face imminent deportation, threatening to flood Nicaragua's impoverished economy, which lacks the infrastructure to absorb them, Roberto Arguello, a Nicaraguan-born banker who sits on the U.S. Senate's Hispanic Task Force, told Reuters.
Arguello's comments contradicted Nicaraguan government and U.S. Embassy statements that no mass deportation was under way or imminent in the near future.
"This is a very serious situation in which the Nicaraguan people have been badly misinformed," said Arguello during a visit to Nicaragua.
The Miami-based Arguello said the effects of tough immigration laws signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton last year will start being felt over the next six months.
"The law is clear. All Nicaraguans who have received deportation letters will be deported," he said.
While Nicaragua wanted to attract educated exiles with capital back to Nicaragua, it clearly feared a mass return of unskilled exiles looking for work.
Nicaragua is the second-poorest country in Latin America with 52 percent of its work force unemployed or underemployed.

"It is certain that we cannot receive at one blow this invasion of Nicaraguans if it comes as an avalanche. The housing infrastructure is precarious and the generation of employment at this moment is almost zero," said Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman, who took power on Jan. 10.
Aleman said he will join Central America's other presidents in asking Clinton when he visits the region in May to temporarily suspend the deportation of Central American illegal immigrants.
"Central America's presidents can say what they want to Clinton but the law is clear in this case," Arguello said.

In the 1970s and 1980s, when the dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza was followed by the left-wing Sandinista government, thousands of Nicaraguans sought political asylum in the United States and abroad.
Arguello said in total almost 25 percent of Nicaragua's population left the country with 200,000 taking up residence in Miami alone.
But with back-to-back democratic elections in Nicaragua and the inauguration of a pro-U.S. government, exiles can no longer claim they face political persecution back home to avoid deportation.
